questions.question: Explain, with South African examples, how the physical causes of flooding differ from the human causes.
questions.expected_answer: Physical causes lie in the rain and the catchment. Rainfall intensity matters more than total — sixty millimetres in ninety minutes outruns the soil's infiltration speed and runs off, where the same amount over a fortnight soaks away — and the interior's summer thunderstorms deliver exactly such bursts. Duration drives the wide-area floods: a cut-off low, a pool of cold upper air that pinches off from the westerlies and stalls, rained for days over Natal in September 1987 and battered the Western Cape through 2023, while tropical systems such as Domoina in 1984 and the remains of Dineo in 2017 flood the north-east. The catchment then decides the storm's fate through antecedent moisture, since saturated soil converts nearly all new rain into runoff; slope, which speeds water to the channels; impermeable rock and thin baked soils; vegetation, whose interception, roots and slow release all reduce runoff; and shape, since a round compact catchment delivers the whole storm to the outlet together. Human causes amplify the hazard and place people inside it: urbanisation seals the ground with tar, paving and roofs while stormwater pipes deliver runoff to rivers at engineered speed, as in the Jukskei's catchment in Johannesburg; deforestation and overgrazing speed runoff and feed eroded sediment onto riverbeds and dam floors, raising channels and shrinking storage; wetland destruction removes the natural sponges that hold and slowly release surges; neglected drains, undersized culverts and unmaintained dams worsen events; and settlement on floodplains — cheap riverside development at one end and informal settlement on the leftover land at the other — puts people on ground the river built and revisits, so that flood exposure in South Africa maps onto poverty.

questions.question: Describe the flood hydrograph fully in words — frame, parts and sequence — and explain both the exact definition of lag time and the asymmetry of the two limbs.
questions.expected_answer: The hydrograph plots time in hours or days on the horizontal axis against discharge on the vertical axis, measured in cubic metres per second, spoken as cumecs, with the storm's rainfall drawn as a block of bars near the origin. Before the rain the trace runs low and flat at base flow — the river's ordinary discharge, supplied by groundwater seeping from saturated ground, which is why rivers flow through the dry months. After the rain begins, the rising limb climbs steeply as the storm's fast water — surface runoff and piped stormwater — reaches the gauge, ending at peak discharge, the highest flow and the moment of greatest danger. Lag time must be defined precisely as the interval between the heaviest rainfall and peak discharge; it represents travel time from where the rain landed, over slopes and along tributaries, to the gauge, and a short lag means the flood arrives before warnings can. The falling or recession limb then descends more gently than the rising limb climbed because the late-arriving water travels by slower routes — seeping laterally through soil and trailing in from the catchment's far edges — before the trace settles onto a base flow slightly above its pre-storm level, since the recharged soil feeds the channel more generously. Interpretation rests on three readings: how high the peak, how short the lag, and how steep the limbs — high, short and steep marking a flashy catchment, low, long and gentle an absorbent one.

questions.question: Contrast the hydrographs of a rural grassland catchment and an urbanised catchment in the same storm, and use the Jukskei flood of December 2022 and the Natal floods of September 1987 to distinguish flash floods from regional floods.
questions.expected_answer: The rural grassland catchment with wetlands and deep soil produces a long lag, because interception and infiltration hold the water back; a low, broad, rounded peak, because much of the storm entered the ground and arrives stretched over time; gentle limbs; and a persistent base flow between storms, because recharged groundwater keeps paying into the channel. The urbanised catchment produces a short lag, because rain lands on roofs and tar and is piped to the channel at design speed; a high narrow peak, the same volume compressed into a fraction of the time; steep limbs; and a starved base flow, because little water reaches the ground. Sealing a catchment raises the peak, shortens the lag and steepens the limbs. The Jukskei event of the third of December 2022 shows the flash flood: an intense storm on the heavily sealed catchment of northern Johannesburg raised the river within minutes on congregants gathered at the water near Alexandra, and at least fourteen people died in a flood that passed within hours. The Natal floods of September 1987 show the regional flood: a stalled cut-off low delivered several hundred millimetres over days onto saturated ground, rivers from the Mgeni northwards spread across their floodplains for days, bridges and roads failed across the province, and more than three hundred people died. Management follows from the hydrograph: lengthen the lag and lower the peak by protecting wetlands, revegetating catchments, choosing permeable surfaces, clearing drains, keeping settlement off floodplains and building warning systems faster than the remaining lag.
